abstract: Multicellular aggregates are initially spherical, yet tissues routinely break this symmetry to form protrusions, invade, and migrate. Whether this symmetry breaking originates within the aggregate or is imposed by its surroundings remains unclear. Here, we embed human mesenchymal stem cell (hMSC) spheroids in synthetic poly(ethylene glycol) hydrogels in which stiffness, viscoelasticity, and degradability are controlled independently. Spheroids in elastic matrices remain spherical; viscoelasticity permits symmetry breaking only in compliant networks, whereas proteolytic degradability permits it in both compliant and rigid matrices. Brillouin microscopy shows that symmetry breaking is accompanied by softening of the spheroid core and loss of internal radial symmetry. Three-dimensional traction force microscopy reveals that the force field is polarised even in spheroids that remain spherical: tractions concentrate at two approximately opposing poles, and focal adhesions adopt a similar bipolar distribution. In spheroids that do break symmetry, protrusions emerge opposite the pole of highest traction. A continuum model shows that an anisotropic distribution of contractile cells is sufficient to reproduce both the patterns and magnitude of the measured displacements. Force polarity is therefore an intrinsic property of the aggregate, whereas matrix mechanics act as a filter that determines whether this polarity is expressed as symmetry breaking.
